top.title: Heavy rain, wind and flooding hit much of US on Thanksgiving
top.summary: Homes left without power and holiday travel disrupted as storms pound east coast and other parts of the US Storms have flooded communities in the US east coast, knocking out power to nearly a million customers and prompting the first-ever postponement of Macy’s Thanksgiving Day parade in New York City. High winds and flooding hammered both coasts, disrupting holiday travel. More than 900,000 homes and businesses were without electricity on Thursday evening, with the majority in east coast states, according to the outage tracking website PowerOutage.us. More than 2,200 flights to or from US destinations were delayed and more than 400 were cancelled, according to the flight tracking service FlightAware. Continue reading...

latest.summary: The constant turnover of players and staff has made consistency an elusive quality at Stamford Bridge Liam Delap came and went. He joined Chelsea in the summer of 2025 and was hailed by Enzo Maresca as the next Harry Kane. Fast forward a year, though, and there was no chance of Delap joining Kane in England’s World Cup squad. The striker’s form was miserable and the only surprise was that Chelsea made a profit when they sold him to Nottingham Forest for £50m last summer. On one level it looks like good business. Delap’s only season at Stamford Bridge featured one serious hamstring injury, one league goal, one ridiculous red card and not much else. latest.title: All Blacks have ‘no gas in the tank’ but stats show it’s England who should be out of juice
latest.summary: Figures indicate England’s players have far more rugby miles in their legs than Saturday’s opponents but Borthwick has managed to balance heavy schedule The prevailing narrative emerging before England’s rematch with New Zealand on Saturday is that the All Blacks are running on fumes. The forwards coach, Jason Ryan, has said that “there is not much juice in the tank” while Graham Henry, who led them to the 2011 World Cup title, has continued the theme in even starker terms. “It’s the end of the season and we’re buggered. They’ve just got no gas in the tank.” It is understood that narrative has raised a number of eyebrows within the England camp. The view, as England seek to clinch a third straight win over New Zealand for the first time in the history of the fixture, is best summed up as, “welcome to our world”. We are nearing the end of a gruelling year for the All Blacks, who give the impression they cannot wait for their season to end, but the grind in England, that which led to Maro Itoje being ordered to take the summer off, is at the very least comparable. Culture.title: The Metaphor Zoo by Jeremy Butterfield review – how animals influence our language
Culture.summary: A lexicographer reveals the surprising origins of common zoological turns of phrase, from fat cats to fur babies Anyone who has grown up in the country knows that cows come home. They do it at tea time, like clockwork, because an unmilked cow is an uncomfortable cow. So how did “till the cows come home” come to mean never? Stranger still, when the phrase first appears in a 1587 commentary on St Paul’s epistle to the Galatians, there is only one cow. By the time playwrights Beaumont and Fletcher take it up a few decades later, their characters are kissing and drinking till the cow – still single – comes home. What began as a promise of endless pleasure has become a sigh of futility. Jeremy Butterfield’s Metaphor Zoo is full of such linguistic metamorphoses. Butterfield is a lexicographer by trade, the man the OUP entrusted with revising Fowler’s Modern English Usage. His guiding text is Lakoff and Johnson’s Metaphors We Live By (1980), which argues that metaphors don’t just colour how we speak but structure our thinking. In this sprightly but well-grounded book (metaphor alert), Butterfield asks what mental patterns lie behind the hundreds of animal phrases in English. Then in Johnsonian fashion, he sets about tracing the original, dating each through the Oxford English Dictionary and watching as it goes walkabout. Continue reading...

Culture.title: ‘Everybody tells me how I can keep working. My answer begins with ‘F’ and ends with ‘off’: Mike Leigh on 55 years of films – and why he’s just made his last
Culture.summary: The acclaimed director has announced his latest film Tender Loving Care will be his last. He talks about coming to terms with a life-changing condition and how he would have loved to have made a big budget modern-day movie Mike Leigh and his partner, the actor Marion Bailey, were knocking around at home last Christmas, looking for a good film to watch and constantly coming up short. Finally, Leigh had a brilliant idea. Why not put on Topsy-Turvy, his 1999 costume romp about the making of The Mikado? Problem solved, perfect choice. “It’s not like a habit,” he says hurriedly. “I don’t sit there watching my films every night like Gloria Swanson in Sunset Boulevard. It’s just that Topsy-Turvy happens to be a very enjoyable watch.” The way Leigh sees it, his films are like children. They’ve outgrown him, moved on, but it’s nice to check the family ties are still strong. Some are sunny (Life is Sweet; Happy-Go-Lucky) and some are dour (Naked; Hard Truths), but they all share the same DNA, the same real-world interests and tragicomic mindset. He can’t choose between them; he’ll defend each one to the death. Then he pauses and says, “But I’ve got a soft spot for Meantime.” Continue reading...

Culture.title: Banish gloom with Paul Foot’s teetering towers of nonsense in fizzy show The Future
Culture.summary: Soho theatre, London The standup throws himself into ‘13 or 14 pieces of humour’ that confirm his gifts for escalating everyday apercus into absurd delights Paul Foot made quite the impression with 2023’s Dissolve , a mid-career breakout from his oddball groove. The Future confirms the 52-year-old as a comic any audience could enjoy, and – to some degree – develops his newfound interest in the real world and the circumstances of his own life. Not that it begins with any seriousness of purpose, as our host throws himself into a series of escalating set pieces built on everyday apercus – how reassuring we find it, say, when a Chinese restaurant is frequented by Chinese diners. Then comes the swerve, which is less well integrated, and less remarkable, than in the show’s predecessor, but affecting nonetheless. Before that, the first half is all about Foot’s free-standing bits (“about 13 or 14 pieces of humour”, he calls them): concentrated bursts of observational comedy, in which he inflates a workaday premise to absurdity and beyond. The etiquette of British funerals; over-excitement at food served on sizzling hot-plates – Foot constructing teetering towers of nonsense from it all with a voice and range of facial expression evoking British comedy at its ooh-missus, nudge-nudge heyday. Continue reading...
